title: Calendar Explorer
context: Grade 3, the last working topic of the time chapter. An adult sees a calendar being flipped, which a paper calendar can do. What is being settled is that a week is always seven days so the same weekday returns every seventh day, that months take turns on the knuckles and in the dips, and that a leap year comes every fourth year and not at random. A child who counts the days between two dates by counting both ends, or who counts forward without taking away the first day, will be one day out and will not see why.

writeup.why: Count the days of a week and the months of a year on a real wall calendar, say the days of each month by the knuckle method, find the leap year as every fourth year, and hop seven days at a time to find a day, a date and the weeks between two dates.
writeup.look: A classroom wall with a real calendar page of 2026 at the left, the month cards, the two fists, the four-year strip and the week counter at the right as each phase needs them, a pencil, flip arrows, a Grid view button, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Calendar Explorer' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many days, weeks or months have been counted so far. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A real wall calendar page hangs at the left of the working area at x 90, y 216, 470 by 440, with a near-black top bar showing the month and the year written large, a header row of the seven days of the week with Sunday first, and a grid of dates in seven columns, the first of the month standing in its true column and a week sharing a row. Two round arrow buttons stand under it at x 90 and x 220, y 668, each 120 by 52, and flip the page like a leaf, and a pencil rests at its right edge. The Grid view button stands at x 360, y 668, 200 by 52, and redraws the page as a plain table. Beside the page, at x 600, y 216, a work area 520 by 440 changes with the phase. On the first phase a row of twelve small month cards, two rows of six each 80 by 70, stands at x 600, y 216, and the week counter, 240 by 100, stands at x 600, y 330. On the second phase two flat drawn fists stand side by side at x 600, y 230, each 240 by 220: the first with four knuckles and three dips labelled January, March, May, July and February, April, June, the second with three knuckles and two dips labelled August, October, December and September, November, and the twelve month cards wait in a row at x 600, y 480, 520 by 90; a card dropped on a knuckle reads thirty-one and on a dip reads thirty, and February is left with its two numbers. On the third phase a four-year strip of four small wall calendars stands at x 600, y 230, 520 by 190, showing their Februaries side by side, the leap year's with a twenty-ninth square ringed in green and labelled Leap year, and the year ruler from 1900 to 2099 in blocks of four runs under it at x 600, y 470, 520 by 90, with a marker the child steps in fours. On the fourth phase the circled date is ringed near-black and the date reached is ringed green, labelled Answer, the seven-day hop lights every seventh date down the same column in one colour, and the week counter stands at x 600, y 470, 260 by 120, counting the weeks between two circled dates in sevens. Real things keep their natural colours throughout, and a date found is never coloured as an hour or a minute. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys and a clear key, for typing a number of days, weeks or months or a year into the answer slot, with a words box that takes the name of a day. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. A clock face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a time is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The calendar page shows the last date circled with the hops lit down its column, and the week counter beside it, with the fists or the strip still in the frame.

phases.win: the twelve pages stack into a year and one extra day sits after the last full week
phases.does: taps a row to count its days, flips through the twelve pages, then counts the weeks in a year and the one day left over
phases.goal: a week has seven days, a year has twelve months and is about fifty-two weeks and one more day
phases.says: Flip the pages of the calendar. How many months make a year?
phases.check: Away from the screen: a school trip lasts some weeks. How would you find how many days that is, and why is a year not exactly fifty-two weeks?
phases.feels: the pages of the year flipping past, and one day left over after the last full week
phases.hands: Hang a real wall calendar, count the days in one row with a finger, flip the pages and count the months, and ask how many weeks fit in the year.
phases.tries: First rung: count the days in one row of the calendar. Second rung: count the rows of seven that make a year. Third rung: the same task with just one month, before the whole year returns.

wrong.why: fifty-two sevens seems to fill the year with no day over
wrong.move: says a year is exactly fifty-two weeks
wrong.screen: the week counter fills with fifty-two full rows of seven, and one lone day is left lit amber on the last page, labelled Left, with the count of days written beside it

wrong.why: twelve months of the same length is easy to multiply
wrong.move: counts the days of the year by adding the twelve months and forgetting that they are not equal
wrong.screen: each month card shows its own number of days when it is tapped, and the counts are added in turn as the pages are flipped

phases.screen: the 2026 wall calendar open at its first month with a row of twelve month cards beside it and the week counter blank
phases.soWhat: a week has seven days, a year has twelve months and is fifty-two weeks and one more day
phases.concept: Days, weeks, months and a year

phases.win: the card lands and its number of days appears, and February is left alone with its two numbers
phases.does: says each month along the fists, drops the card on a knuckle or a dip, and reads the number of days
phases.goal: months take turns on the knuckles and in the dips: a knuckle month has thirty-one days and a dip month thirty
phases.says: Say the months along the knuckles and the dips. Which months have thirty-one days?
phases.check: Away from the screen: make a fist and say the months. Is the month your birthday is in on a knuckle or in a dip, and how many days does it have?
phases.feels: the months falling onto knuckles and dips in turn, with February left alone
phases.hands: Make a fist and say the months along the knuckles and the dips, then fold a paper strip into twelve boxes, mark the knuckle months and write the days in each.
phases.tries: First rung: say the months along the fist from January. Second rung: say whether the month you stopped on is a knuckle or a dip. Third rung: the same task with the first four months only, before the rest return.

wrong.why: the first months said, January and March, have thirty-one, so it feels like all of them
wrong.move: says a dip month has thirty-one days
wrong.screen: the month card is dropped on the dip and its number reads thirty, and the knuckle months light in turn along the fist with thirty-one beside each

wrong.why: two fists look like two sets of months
wrong.move: counts the knuckles and dips as if the months sat in two separate rows
wrong.screen: the months are said along the first fist and then, without a gap, along the second, so July and August both sit on a knuckle and the count carries on

phases.screen: two drawn fists with four knuckles and three dips on the first and three knuckles and two dips on the second, and twelve month cards waiting
phases.soWhat: a knuckle month has thirty-one days, a dip month has thirty, and February has twenty-eight or twenty-nine
phases.concept: How many days in a month: the knuckle method

phases.win: the twenty-ninth square drops into the leap February and the year ruler lights every fourth year
phases.does: counts in fours on the year ruler from a leap year, taps the February that grows a twenty-ninth square, and finds a year from the last and the next leap years
phases.goal: every fourth year is a leap year, and its February has an extra day and the year has one day more
phases.says: Look at the four Februaries. Which one has an extra day?
phases.check: Away from the screen: this year is a leap year. In how many years is the next one, and how many days does February have in it?
phases.feels: the extra day dropping into one February in four
phases.hands: Fold a paper strip into four boxes, one for each year, draw February in each, give one an extra day, and count in fours from a leap year on a number line of years.
phases.tries: First rung: step the marker four years from a leap year. Second rung: check that the year you land on is a leap year. Third rung: the same task with the last leap year only, before the next one returns.

wrong.why: the leap years seen so far all happened to have even numbers
wrong.move: says every year that ends in an even number is a leap year
wrong.screen: the year ruler lights every fourth year only, and the years between it stay dark even when their numbers are even

wrong.why: three or five seems close enough to a few years
wrong.move: counts in threes or fives instead of fours from a leap year
wrong.screen: the marker steps four years at a time along the ruler, and the February on the strip grows its extra square only at every fourth step

phases.screen: a four-year strip of small wall calendars with their Februaries side by side, and a year ruler from nineteen hundred to two thousand ninety-nine
phases.soWhat: every fourth year is a leap year, with twenty-nine days in February and three hundred and sixty-six days in the year
phases.concept: Leap year: every fourth year has 366 days

phases.win: the hops light the same weekday down the column and the week counter shows the weeks between the two dates
phases.does: circles a date, hops seven days at a time down the column, then counts on to the date asked for or counts the weeks between two circled dates
phases.goal: the same day of the week comes back every seven days, so a day or a date is found by hopping in sevens
phases.says: Circle the date. Hop seven days and see which day lights up each time.
phases.check: Away from the screen: a plant was put in a pot on a Monday. What day of the week is it three weeks later, and how do you know?
phases.feels: the same weekday lighting down the column, one week at a time
phases.hands: Circle a date on a real wall calendar with a pencil, count seven days along with a finger and see which day you land on, then count the days to a second date and change them into weeks.
phases.tries: First rung: hop seven days once. Second rung: hop again and say the day each time. Third rung: the same task with one hop only, before more hops return.

wrong.why: counting both ends feels natural when pointing at dates
wrong.move: counts the days between two dates including the first date
wrong.screen: the first date is ringed near-black and left out of the count, the days are counted from the next date on, and the week counter shows the total

wrong.why: a week is easy to mix up with the days that make it
wrong.move: hops six days or eight days instead of seven
wrong.screen: each hop lands on a date lit in one colour, and a hop of six or eight leaves a different weekday lit, so the seventh is seen to be the one that stays

phases.screen: a calendar page with a pencil, a seven-day hop and a week counter, and one date already circled
phases.soWhat: the same day of the week comes back every seven days, so a day or a date is found by hopping in sevens
phases.concept: Finding a day and a date on a calendar

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when the pencil circles a date, the seven-day hop jumps down the calendar one week at a time, lighting the same weekday in the same colour with a small tick each time it lands. On the third phase, the leap February squeezes in its twenty-ninth square with a soft click, and the other three Februaries stay as they were.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the 2026 wall calendar is open at its first month, a row of twelve month cards lies beside it and the week counter is blank. On the second the two drawn fists stand beside the calendar with their knuckles and dips labelled and the twelve month cards waiting. On the third a four-year strip of small wall calendars shows its Februaries side by side, and the year ruler is lit at one leap year. On the fourth a calendar page has one date circled with the pencil, the seven-day hop is lit but has not yet moved, and the week counter is empty. One thing moves, once: the first page, or the circled date on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any month of the 2026 calendar, the two fists with every month card, the four-year strip and the year ruler, any circled date with the seven-day hop, and the Grid view. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the months of a year, the knuckle method, the leap year and finding a day or a date, each in a real situation.
voiceLines: A calendar on the wall, waiting to be flipped.
Flip the pages of the calendar. How many months make a year?
Say the months along the knuckles and the dips. Which months have thirty-one days?
Look at the four Februaries. Which one has an extra day?
Circle the date. Hop seven days and see which day lights up each time.
A new page. Find the day first.
Free play. Flip, hop and count as you like.
Count again, one week or one month at a time.
You found each day by counting weeks and months.

observations.why: a week has seven days, so seven days after a date is the same day of the week.
observations.soWhat: hopping seven days at a time finds the same weekday again and again.
observations.observe: Every seventh date down one column lit in the same colour on the calendar page.

observations.why: the months take turns on the knuckles and in the dips, with February left alone.
observations.soWhat: the knuckle method gives the days of every month except February.
observations.observe: A card dropped on a knuckle read thirty-one and on a dip read thirty.

observations.why: an extra day is added to February every fourth year.
observations.soWhat: every fourth year is a leap year, with twenty-nine days in February and one more day in the year.
observations.observe: One February on the four-year strip grew a twenty-ninth square, once in four years.

observations.why: fifty-two weeks is three hundred and sixty-four days and a year has one day more.
observations.soWhat: a year is fifty-two weeks and one more day, not fifty-two weeks alone.
observations.observe: The week counter counted fifty-two weeks in a year and one day was left over.

source_tool.description: A real wall calendar page of 2026 hangs on a classroom wall at the left of the working area. It has a near-black top bar with the month and the year written large, a header row of the seven days of the week with Sunday first, and a grid of days in seven columns, the first of the month standing in its true column and the days of one week sharing a row. Two round buttons, an arrow left and an arrow right, flip the page like a leaf, and a pencil rests beside it. On the first phase a row of twelve small month cards lies beside the page, and tapping a row of the page counts its seven days. On the second phase two flat drawn fists stand beside the calendar, with their knuckles and dips labelled, and the child drops each month card on a knuckle or a dip, and the card reads thirty-one or thirty. On the third phase a four-year strip of four small wall calendars shows their Februaries side by side, and the leap year has a twenty-ninth square ringed in green; a year ruler from 1900 to 2099 in blocks of four lets the child step from one leap year to the next. On the fourth phase a pencil circles a date, a seven-day hop lights every seventh date down the same column in one colour, and a week counter counts the weeks between two circled dates. A number pad types a number of days, weeks, or a year, and a words box takes the name of a day. A Grid view button redraws the page as a plain table. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many days, weeks or months have been counted.
source_tool.art_direction: A classroom wall with a real calendar

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a wall clock with its numbers, a wristwatch, a digital alarm clock, a school bell, a stopwatch, a sunrise over a school, a street lamp at night, a wall calendar page, a birthday card, a football, a film ticket. The object is the thing the child reads or sets, and a plain dial or a bare number appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

Every clock is drawn exactly: twelve numbers, sixty minute marks with a longer mark at every fifth, the minute hand turning six degrees a minute and the hour hand thirty degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute, so the hour hand sits between two numbers whenever the minutes are not zero. Neither hand has an arrowhead, and the two hands never lie on top of each other in a picture that asks the child to read them.
A time is always written the way it is said: 7:20, quarter past 7, 7:20 a.m. A.m. and p.m. are written with the time and never alone, and noon and midnight are never given an a.m. or a p.m.

A length of time is drawn as a bar or a band laid along a clock or a day strip from its start to its end, so the child sees how long, and a band that crosses noon is drawn through the noon mark in two pieces.
A date is written in boxes: a day box, a month box and a year box, and a day is never written without its month and year.
A calendar page is a grid of seven columns headed with the days of the week, Sunday first, and its first day starts in the right column.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a number or a day the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a wall clock keeps its frame and a school bell stays brass. The hour hand of a clock is vermilion and the minute hand is deep blue, because a hand is a mark that stands for a number, on a clock whose face, rim and numbers are near-black on cream, and the hours are vermilion and the minutes deep blue everywhere else, in a digital time, a label and a tag. The a.m. half of a day, from midnight to noon, is sky blue, and the p.m. half, from noon to midnight, is amber. The time reached, a length of time worked out, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Hour hand, Minute hand, a.m., p.m. and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Count again, one week or one month at a time.
voice.onNext: A new page. Find the day first.
voice.opening: A calendar on the wall, waiting to be flipped.
voice.onFinish: You found each day by counting weeks and months.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Flip, hop and count as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Days, weeks, months and a year
How many days in a month: the knuckle method
Leap year: every fourth year has 366 days
Finding a day and a date on a calendar

placement.where: After the class has looked at a real wall calendar together, found their own birthdays and said the knuckle months along their own fists, and before the leap year is named. The tool is what lets one February grow a twenty-ninth square on a four-year strip and what hops seven days down a column again and again, which a paper calendar cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: A week has seven days and a year has twelve months. A year is about fifty-two weeks and one more day, because fifty-two weeks is three hundred and sixty-four days and a year has three hundred and sixty-five. A month has twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty or thirty-one days. On the knuckles, a knuckle month has thirty-one days, a dip month has thirty days, and February has twenty-eight, or twenty-nine in a leap year. Every fourth year is a leap year, with twenty-nine days in February and three hundred and sixty-six days in the year. Adding seven days to a date gives the same day of the week, so the days between two dates are changed into weeks by counting in sevens, and a date a few days after a known day is found by counting on from that day.
answer_key.wrong: The calendar page is shown again with the dates counted along the column, a small number landing on each in turn, and the child's answer ringed on a second page beside it, so the two counts are seen side by side. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

steps: So the school trip lasts 28 days.
items.question: A school trip lasts 4 weeks. How many days is that?
items.checkpoint: A week has 7 days, so count the days in sevens.
items.misconception: Adding 4 and 7 to get 11 days instead of making 4 groups of 7 days.

steps: Say the months along the knuckles in turn: January is a knuckle, February is a dip, March is a knuckle, April is a dip, May is a knuckle, June is a dip, July is a knuckle.
So July is a knuckle month.
A knuckle month has 31 days, so July has 31 days.
items.answer: A knuckle month. July has 31 days.
items.question: A summer holiday lasts all through July. On the knuckles, is July a knuckle month or a dip month, and how many days does it have?
items.checkpoint: Knuckle months have 31 days and dip months have 30 days.
items.misconception: Calling July a dip month because it comes after June, which is a dip, and forgetting to count along the knuckles from January.

steps: A leap year comes every fourth year.
Count in fours from a leap year: 2040 is a leap year, and 2040 plus 4 is 2044.
In a leap year February has 29 days.
items.answer: 29 days, because 2044 is a leap year
items.question: A school wall calendar is printed for the year 2044. Does February have 28 or 29 days in that year?
items.checkpoint: Every fourth year is a leap year, and its February has an extra day.
items.misconception: Saying February always has 28 days, whatever the year.

steps: Count the days from 3 October to 31 October: 31 minus 3 is 28 days.
28 days is 4 weeks, because 4 times 7 is 28.
items.question: A plant is put in a pot on 3 October 2026 and its first flower opens on 31 October 2026. How many weeks did the plant take?
items.checkpoint: Find how many days pass, then count them in sevens.
items.misconception: Counting 31 days and forgetting to take away the first 3 days.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A wall calendar has one page for each month of the year. How many pages does it have?
items.final_answer: 12 pages, one for each of the 12 months

items.question: A school term ends in June. On the knuckles, is June a knuckle month or a dip month, and how many days does it have?
items.final_answer: A dip month. June has 30 days.

items.question: A birthday card says 29 February. Which year has a 29 February, 2046 or 2048?
items.final_answer: 2048, because 2048 is a leap year and 2046 is not a leap year

items.question: A story book from the school library is borrowed on a Friday and is due in 2 weeks. On which day of the week is it due?
items.final_answer: Friday, because 2 weeks is 14 days and 14 days later is the same day of the week

items.question: A bus pass lasts one whole year. A year is 52 weeks and 1 more day. How many days does the pass last?
items.final_answer: 365 days, because 52 weeks is 364 days and 1 more day makes 365

items.question: A train runs every day through September and October. Which month has more days, and how many more?
items.final_answer: October has 1 more day. October is a knuckle month with 31 days and September is a dip month with 30 days.

items.question: A school notice says that last year was a leap year and that the next leap year will be 2048. What year is it now?
items.final_answer: 2045, because the leap year before 2048 is 2044, last year was 2044 and this year is 1 year later

items.question: Use the 2026 calendar. A school exam is on 24 June 2026, and 1 June 2026 is a Monday. On which day of the week is the exam?
items.final_answer: Wednesday, because 22 June is a Monday and 24 June is 2 days later

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: flip the wall calendar to the next or the earlier month
twelve cards that are counted, and dropped on a knuckle or a dip
two drawn fists whose knuckles and dips take the month cards and show thirty-one or thirty
shows four Februaries side by side and steps from one leap year to the next
circles a date on the calendar page
lights every seventh date down the same column in one colour
counts the weeks between two circled dates
redraws the wall calendar page as a plain table of dates
types a number of days, weeks or months, or a year

teaching_notes: Hang a real wall calendar in the room before the tool opens, and let the class find their own birthdays and the first day of the year. Say the knuckle months along fists together, and ask each child to count the days of one month for themselves. Fold a paper strip into four years and mark the leap year to show why one February is longer. Insist on counting the days between two dates by taking the first date away, and wait for a child to say why the same day comes back after seven days, rather than saying it for them. If a child says a year is exactly fifty-two weeks, ask how many days that is. Use fresh dates: the printed exercise asks about the calendar of the year, and the child's own answers come from the page in front of them.
generation_prompt: Build a calendar tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, a classroom wall with real things drawn as recognisable flat illustrations in their natural colours. A real wall calendar page of the year 2026 hangs at the left of the working area with a near-black top bar showing the month and the year, a header row of the seven days of the week, Sunday first, and a grid of dates in seven columns with the first of the month in its true column; two arrow buttons flip the page like a leaf, and a pencil rests beside it. On the first phase a row of twelve month cards sits beside the page and a tap on a row counts its seven days. On the second phase two flat drawn fists with labelled knuckles and dips take the month cards, which show thirty-one or thirty. On the third phase a four-year strip of four small wall calendars shows their Februaries side by side, with a twenty-ninth square ringed in green on the leap year, and a year ruler from 1900 to 2099 in blocks of four. On the fourth phase the pencil circles a date, a seven-day hop lights every seventh date down the same column, and a week counter counts the weeks between two circled dates. A Grid view button redraws the page as a plain table. A number pad types days, weeks or a year, and a words box takes the name of a day. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the days, weeks or months counted. No people or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Flip the pages of the calendar. Say the months along the knuckles. Find the leap year. Hop seven days to find the same day.
